Unusually high or energized? I mean... no, not really. Not for days at a time. I mean, don't get me wrong, in my line of work, you get these massive adrenaline dumps, right?

Drugs? Oh, man, no. Absolutely not. I mean, first off, I'm a firefighter, so we get random drops—drug tests, I mean—all the time. But even if we didn't, you just can't be messed up doing what I do, you know? You're holding someone's life in your hands, pulling them out of a
Do your symptoms tend to happen after you’ve been drinking alcohol?

Alcohol? No, definitely not. I mean, I'll have a beer every now and then, sure. Like, if we just got off a really brutal 48-hour shift and a few of the guys from the house want to grab a drink to decompress... because, you know, when you've been running calls all night, your brain is just totally fried but also completely wired at the same time, if that makes sense? You kind of need a minute to just sit and look at a wall before you go home to your family. 

But I'm not a heavy drinker by any stretch. And the stuff I'm dealing with—the constant pacing, the losing track of what I'm doing in the middle of doing it, just the sheer noise in my head—that's happening all the time. Morning, noon, and night. It really doesn't matter if I've had a beer with the guys
Do you worry a lot about many different things, not just the schedule problems at work?
Worry? I mean... no, not really. I wouldn't call myself a worrier. I don't sit around stressing about, you know, the economy or the future or getting sick or whatever it is
Have these symptoms continued for more than six months after the schedule changes became the new normal at work?

Yeah, oh yeah, definitely. I mean, the schedule change... that was a while ago now. It's been, what, a year and five months? Something like that. I remember exactly when it started because it was right around the time they rolled out this whole new protocol for the longer rotating shifts, which, let me tell you, threw everyone for a loop. But it wasn't just the shifts, you know? They piled on all this extra documentation we had to do after every single call. Used to be you'd write up a quick report, boom, done, back in service. Now it's like you need a law degree to fill out the paperwork. 

And then, on top of all that, they decided our house was going to be the one to pilot the new drone program. Which sounds cool, right? Flying drones to scout out structural fires or hazmat situations. But the reality is it's just another massive thing to keep track of—the maintenance logs, the battery cycles, the flight hours. It's endless. So, yeah, ever since all of that hit about a year and a half ago, it's just been a total nightmare trying to keep my head above water. I thought I'd get used to it, you know? Like, you adapt, right? That's what we do. But it hasn't gotten any better. If anything, it's just been this constant, grinding struggle every single day since they made all those changes.
Have these symptoms been causing problems in your daily functioning?

Yeah. Yeah, it really has. I mean, it's gotten to the point where it's not just me being frustrated with myself anymore. It's bleeding into how the guys see me, and in a firehouse, trust is literally everything. If they can't trust you, you're a liability. 

Like, just last week, my captain actually pulled me into the office for a formal performance and safety meeting. A safety meeting. Me. I've been doing this for over a decade, and I've always prided myself on being the guy people can rely on when things go sideways. But during the meeting, he brought up all these little things I've been dropping the ball on—forgetting to log the drone battery cycles, missing steps in the new documentation, misplacing the rig keys... just stupid, careless mistakes that I never used to make. He wasn't mean about it, but he was serious. He basically said that if I can't keep track of the details in the station, how can the crew trust me to keep track of the details on a call when lives are on the line? 

And that just... man, that gutted me. Because he's right. And the worst part is, I've been working my tail off trying to get promoted to lieutenant. I've put in the time, I've taken the classes, I know the job inside and out. But now? I can feel that leadership spot just completely slipping through my fingers. Why would they promote a guy who can't even remember to plug in a radio battery? It's like I'm watching my career stall out right in front of me, and no matter how hard I try to just focus and get it together, I keep messing up the small stuff. So, yeah... it's definitely causing problems. Big ones.
Before age 12, did you often have trouble paying attention, staying organized, or keeping track of things?

Well, yeah. I mean, my mom actually brought this up recently when I was telling her about the whole mess at work. She was like, "You know you were exactly like this back in grade school, right?" And honestly, she's not wrong. I remember it being a whole thing. Like, I was always the kid who just could not stay in his seat. The teacher would be up there talking, and I'd be up wandering over to the pencil sharpener, or checking out the class pet, or just standing up at my desk for no reason. 

And the blurting out answers... man, that drove my teachers crazy. I just couldn't wait to be called on. The thought would pop into my head and boom, it was out of my mouth before I even realized my hand wasn't raised. And the homework... don't even get me started on the homework. It wasn't that I couldn't do it. I was a smart kid, you know? I grasped the material fine. But I'd do the worksheet, shove it in my desk or my backpack, and then the next day when it was time to turn it in? Gone. Vanished. It was like a black hole in my desk. 

My mom got so many notes sent home. I mean, constantly. "He's bright, but he doesn't apply himself," or "He needs to focus," or "He's disrupting the class." It was always something. She tried color-coded folders, checklists on the fridge, everything. Nothing really stuck. I just kind of scraped by because I could pass the tests, but the day-to-day stuff, the organization, just keeping my head on straight... it was a disaster even back then. So, yeah, it's definitely not a new thing, even if it feels like it's ruining my life more now than it did when I was nine.
